scenes.head: Relative valuation
scenes.sub: Value a share by the price the market puts on similar companies: P/E, EV/EBITDA, EV/EBIT, price-to-book, PEG and dividend yield, why equity and enterprise multiples must never be mixed, how to choose peers, and why two companies in the same trade deserve different multiples.

segs.say: Relative valuation. Value a share by the price the market puts on similar companies: P/E, EV/EBITDA, EV/EBIT, price-to-book, PEG and dividend yield, why equity and enterprise multiples must never be mixed, how to choose peers, and why two companies in the same trade deserve different multiples.

scenes.head: You will be able to

segs.say: Calculate P/E, EV/EBITDA, EV/EBIT, price-to-book, PEG and dividend yield, and say which are equity multiples and which enterprise multiples.
Estimate a company’s value by applying peer multiples, bridging an enterprise value to equity, without mixing the two kinds.
Choose a peer group and explain the judgements it involves.
Explain why multiples differ between companies, using the Gordon-implied P/E and price-to-book with growth, risk and payout.
Evaluate a relative valuation for common pitfalls: negative or one-off earnings, mismatched peers and a market that is itself mispriced.

scenes.head: The DCF in the previous lesson took a five-year forecast, a WACC and a guess about growth for ever to value Morrow & Pike Roasters at $30.14 a share.

segs.say: The DCF in the previous lesson took a five-year forecast, a WACC and a guess about growth for ever to value Morrow & Pike Roasters at $30.14 a share. Ana’s accountant, who has bought and sold a few small businesses, says practitioners rarely start there. “What are similar companies selling for? Start with that.” This lesson does what he suggests, with the two fictional listed companies the course uses, Morrow & Pike and Harbour Street Foods, and then uses them to price a private café chain.

scenes.head: A valuation multiple divides a measure of value by a measure of what the company earns or owns: price by earnings per share, enterprise value by…

segs.say: A valuation multiple divides a measure of value by a measure of what the company earns or owns: price by earnings per share, enterprise value by EBITDA, market capitalisation by book equity. If similar companies trade at a similar multiple, the multiple of one can price another. Estate agents do the same with price per square metre; nobody would value a flat by forecasting its rents for ever when three similar flats sold last month.

scenes.head: This is relative valuation: it says what a company is worth compared with others, not what it is worth absolutely.

segs.say: This is relative valuation: it says what a company is worth compared with others, not what it is worth absolutely. If the whole sector is overpriced, a company priced in line with its peers is overpriced too. A DCF asks “what is the cash worth?”; a multiple asks “what is the market paying for similar cash?”. Each checks the other, and the next lesson combines them.
Morrow & Pike and Harbour Street at 31 December 2027 (fictional)

scenes.head: A multiple is a compressed DCF

segs.say: A multiple is a compressed DCF. A multiple hides the same assumptions a DCF states: growth, risk and how much the company must reinvest. Paying 18 times earnings is a bet on growth and risk just as surely as a terminal growth rate is. The advantage of a multiple is that the market has already made the bet for similar companies; the danger is forgetting that it is a bet.

scenes.head: Every multiple has a numerator (a value) and a denominator (a flow or a stock).

segs.say: Every multiple has a numerator (a value) and a denominator (a flow or a stock). The rule that prevents most errors is that both must belong to the same claimants. An equity multiple puts the shareholders’ value (the share price, or market capitalisation) over something that belongs to shareholders: earnings after interest, book equity, dividends. An enterprise value multiple puts the value of the whole business (enterprise value) over something that belongs to lenders and shareholders together: revenue, EBITDA, EBIT.

P/E ratio. Price ÷ earnings per share. Morrow & Pike: 28.00 ÷ 1.556 = 18.0. Equity multiple; earnings are after interest, so it depends on the firm’s debt. The trailing P/E uses the last year’s earnings; the forward P/E uses next year’s forecast: Morrow & Pike’s is 28.00 ÷ (1.556 × 1.08) = 16.7.

EV/EBITDA. Enterprise value ÷ EBITDA. Morrow & Pike: 1,258 ÷ 118 = 10.7. Enterprise multiple; unaffected by how the firm is financed or by its depreciation policy, which is why acquirers like it. It ignores the capital spending a business needs, so a company that must reinvest heavily looks cheaper than it is.
EV/EBIT. Enterprise value ÷ EBIT. Morrow & Pike: 1,258 ÷ 92 = 13.7. Enterprise multiple that charges depreciation as a rough proxy for the cost of replacing assets.

Price-to-book. Market capitalisation ÷ book equity (the market-to-book ratio). Morrow & Pike: 1,120 ÷ 520 = 2.15. Equity multiple; most useful where assets are marked close to market value (banks, insurers) and least where value lies in brands and people.

PEG ratio. P/E ÷ expected earnings growth in percent. Morrow & Pike: 18.0 ÷ 8 = 2.25. A rough way to compare P/Es of companies growing at different rates; it ignores risk and how long the growth lasts.
Dividend yield. Dividend per share ÷ price. Morrow & Pike: 0.70 ÷ 28.00 = 2.50%. Equity measure, the inverse of a price-to-dividend multiple.

scenes.head: Which multiple to use depends on the business.

segs.say: Which multiple to use depends on the business. EV/EBITDA suits companies with similar capital needs and different debt, which is why it dominates takeovers. EV/EBIT is better when capital intensity differs, because depreciation stands in for the cost of keeping the assets working: Morrow & Pike spends 4.5% of its revenue on equipment, Harbour Street 3.2%. P/E is the most quoted and the easiest to explain, and suits companies with similar debt and steady profits. Price-to-book suits businesses whose assets are financial. EV/revenue (Morrow & Pike 1.66, Harbour Street 0.84) is a last resort for companies with no profit yet, since it says nothing about margins: Morrow & Pike’s higher EV/revenue mostly reflects its higher EBIT margin, 12.1% against 7.4%.

scenes.head: Mixing the two kinds gives nonsense, and it is easy to do by accident.

segs.say: Mixing the two kinds gives nonsense, and it is easy to do by accident. Apply a P/E to EBITDA and you price the lenders’ share of the cash as if it belonged to the shareholders, and before depreciation too. Apply EV/EBITDA and stop there, and you have the value of the whole business, not of the shares: subtract debt and add cash first. The lesson’s worked example shows both slips on a private café chain.

chapters.title: Why Morrow & Pike trades at more than Harbour Street

scenes.head: Morrow & Pike sells at 18.0 times earnings and Harbour Street at 12.7.

segs.say: Morrow & Pike sells at 18.0 times earnings and Harbour Street at 12.7. Is Harbour Street cheap? Not necessarily: a multiple should be higher for a company that grows faster, is less risky or needs to reinvest less of its earnings to grow. The Gordon model makes this exact. If P₀ = D₁ ÷ (r_E − g) and the dividend is a share of earnings, dividing both sides by this year’s EPS gives the P/E the model justifies:
P₀/E₀ = (Payout × (1 + g))/(r_E − g), g = (1 − Payout) × ROE

scenes.head: For Morrow & Pike: payout 45.0%, ROE 12.0%, so g = 6.59%; cost of equity 9.15% (beta 0.90).

segs.say: For Morrow & Pike: payout 45.0%, ROE 12.0%, so g = 6.59%; cost of equity 9.15% (beta 0.90). The justified P/E is 0.450 × 1.0659 ÷ (9.15% − 6.59%) = 18.7, close to the 18.0 it trades at. For Harbour Street: payout 42.5%, ROE 10.3%, so g = 5.91%; cost of equity 11.08% (beta 1.25). Its justified P/E is 0.425 × 1.0591 ÷ (11.08% − 5.91%) = 8.7, well below its 12.7.

scenes.head: Multiplying the justified P/E by ROE (this year’s earnings ÷ book equity) gives the justified price-to-book, P₀ ÷ B₀ = ROE × P₀ ÷ E₀.

segs.say: Multiplying the justified P/E by ROE (this year’s earnings ÷ book equity) gives the justified price-to-book, P₀ ÷ B₀ = ROE × P₀ ÷ E₀. A company earning about its cost of equity is worth about its book value; above it, more; below it, less. Morrow & Pike’s is 12.0% × 18.7 = 2.24 against 2.15 in the market. Harbour Street earns 10.3% on its equity but its shareholders require 11.08%, so the model says it is worth less than book: 10.3% × 8.7 = 0.89, against 1.31 in the market. (With ROE measured as next year’s earnings ÷ book equity now, the same result is often written (ROE − g) ÷ (r_E − g).)

scenes.head: So the gap in multiples is partly justified (Harbour Street is riskier, grows more slowly and earns less on its equity) and partly not: the market…

segs.say: So the gap in multiples is partly justified (Harbour Street is riskier, grows more slowly and earns less on its equity) and partly not: the market prices Harbour Street well above what its current return on equity supports. Either investors expect its returns to improve, or the shares are expensive, not cheap. A low multiple is a question, not an answer. The fundamental analysis lesson takes up Harbour Street’s case.

scenes.head: Multiples in the real market differ by industry

segs.say: Multiples in the real market differ by industry. Damodaran’s table of US enterprise value multiples for January 2026 puts EV/EBITDA for food processing firms with positive EBITDA at 10.01 and for restaurant and dining firms at 17.49. Industries differ in growth, risk and how much capital they need, and their multiples differ with them. That is why peers should come from the same business, and why a multiple borrowed from another industry means little.

scenes.head: The peer group decides the answer more than the arithmetic does.

segs.say: The peer group decides the answer more than the arithmetic does. Good peers share the target’s business model, growth, risk, size and accounting basis. In practice no peer matches on everything, and the analyst trades closeness against number: two close peers may be better than ten loose ones, but a single peer’s multiple carries all its own quirks. Morrow & Pike (a roaster) and Harbour Street (a packaged-food maker) are both in coffee but neither runs cafés. Brightcup Coffee, the closest listed café chain, is the course project’s subject and is left out here.

scenes.head: Having chosen peers, use the median rather than the mean when there are several (one outlier can move a mean a long way), look at the range as well…

segs.say: Having chosen peers, use the median rather than the mean when there are several (one outlier can move a mean a long way), look at the range as well as the middle, and adjust for known differences rather than applying the middle blindly. Use the same year for every company, trailing or forward, and the same definition of earnings: if one company’s profit includes a one-off gain, strip it out before comparing.
Negative or tiny earnings. A P/E is meaningless when earnings are negative and enormous when they are close to zero. Use an enterprise multiple of revenue or EBITDA instead, or a forward multiple.
Cycles. At the top of a cycle earnings are high and P/Es look low; at the bottom the reverse. Normalised (average-cycle) earnings help.
Accounting differences. Different depreciation lives, one-off items and how leases or acquisitions are treated move earnings and EBITDA; compare on the same basis.
The whole market can be wrong. Relative valuation inherits whatever the market believes about the sector. In a sector-wide boom every company looks fairly priced against its peers.

Control and liquidity. Listed multiples price small, easily sold stakes. A buyer of a whole private company gets control but cannot sell easily; how far these offset each other is a judgement, and practitioners argue about it.

scenes.head: Price-to-earnings ratio

segs.say: Price-to-earnings ratio: P/E = P/EPS = (Market capitalisation)/(Net income).
P: Share price ($).
EPS: Earnings per share: net income ÷ shares (last year for trailing, next year for forward) ($).
It assumes this: Earnings are positive and free of one-off items.

scenes.head: Enterprise value multiples

segs.say: Enterprise value multiples: EV/EBITDA, EV/EBIT, EV = Market capitalisation + Debt − Cash.
EV: Enterprise value ($).
EBITDA: Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation ($).
EBIT: Earnings before interest and tax ($).
It assumes this: Numerator and denominator both belong to lenders and shareholders together.

scenes.head: Value implied by a peer multiple

segs.say: Value implied by a peer multiple: Equity = m_(EV) × Metric − Debt + Cash or Equity = m_(eq) × Metric.
m_(EV): A peer enterprise multiple (EV/EBITDA, EV/EBIT) (×).
m_(eq): A peer equity multiple (P/E, price-to-book) (×).
Metric: The target’s matching figure (EBITDA, EBIT, net income, book equity) ($).
Debt, Cash: The target’s debt and cash ($).
Equity: The value of the target’s shares ($).
It assumes this: The peers are comparable in growth, risk and reinvestment; the market prices them fairly.

scenes.head: PEG ratio

segs.say: PEG ratio: PEG = (P/E)/(100 × g).
P/E: Price-to-earnings ratio (×).
g: Expected annual growth in earnings per share, usually over the next five years.
It assumes this: A rough adjustment for growth only; it ignores risk and how long growth lasts.

scenes.head: Justified (Gordon-implied) P/E and price-to-book

segs.say: Justified (Gordon-implied) P/E and price-to-book: P₀/E₀ = (Payout (1 + g))/(r_E − g), P₀/B₀ = ROE × P₀/E₀.
P₀: Share price ($).
E₀: This year’s earnings per share ($).
B₀: Book equity per share ($).
Payout: Dividends ÷ earnings.
g: Constant growth: (1 − payout) × ROE (% per year).
ROE: Return on equity: this year’s earnings ÷ book equity (% per year).
r_E: Cost of equity (% per year).
It assumes this: The Gordon model’s: constant growth, payout and ROE for ever, with g below r_E.

chapters.title: Example: Harbour Street’s multiples from its accounts

scenes.head: Harbour Street’s multiples from its accounts

segs.say: Harbour Street Foods trades at $18.00 with 120 million shares. In 2027 it earned net income of $169.5 million, EBITDA of $410 million and EBIT of $290 million; it has $1,188 million of debt and $60 million of cash. Find its P/E, enterprise value and EV/EBITDA.

scenes.head: Harbour Street’s multiples from its accounts

segs.say: Step 1. Market capitalisation: 18.00 × 120 = $2,160 million. EPS: 169.5 ÷ 120 = $1.4125.
Step 3. Enterprise value: 2,160 + 1,188 − 60 = $3,288 million.

scenes.head: Harbour Street’s multiples from its accounts

segs.say: P/E 12.7; enterprise value $3,288 million; EV/EBITDA 8.0.

Debt is more than a third of Harbour Street’s enterprise value, so its P/E and its EV/EBITDA tell different stories: the P/E reflects earnings after a large interest bill, the EV multiple the business before financing.

chapters.title: Example: Is Harbour Street cheap at 12.7 times earnings?

scenes.head: Is Harbour Street cheap at 12.7 times earnings?

segs.say: Harbour Street’s P/E (12.7) is well below Morrow & Pike’s (18.0). Use the Gordon-implied P/E to judge whether the gap is justified. Harbour Street: payout 42.5%, ROE 10.3%, beta 1.25. Morrow & Pike: payout 45.0%, ROE 12.0%, beta 0.90. Risk-free rate 4.2%, market risk premium 5.5%.

scenes.head: Is Harbour Street cheap at 12.7 times earnings?

segs.say: Step 1. Costs of equity: Harbour Street 4.2% + 1.25 × 5.5% = 11.08%; Morrow & Pike 4.2% + 0.90 × 5.5% = 9.15%.
Step 2. Growth from retention: Harbour Street 0.575 × 10.3% = 5.91%; Morrow & Pike 0.550 × 12.0% = 6.59%.
Step 4. Compare with the market: Morrow & Pike trades close to its justified multiple (18.0 against 18.7); Harbour Street trades well above its own (12.7 against 8.7).

scenes.head: Is Harbour Street cheap at 12.7 times earnings?

segs.say: The model justifies a P/E of about 8.7 for Harbour Street and 18.7 for Morrow & Pike. Harbour Street’s lower multiple is more than explained by its higher risk and lower return on equity; on these inputs it is not cheap.

A lower multiple than a peer’s is not a bargain if the company is riskier and less profitable. The market may expect Harbour Street’s return on equity to improve; an investor who buys it as “cheap” is really betting on that improvement.

chapters.title: Example: Pricing a private café chain from listed peers

scenes.head: Pricing a private café chain from listed peers

segs.say: Copperkettle Coffee (fictional) owns 38 cafés and is for sale. In 2027 it made EBITDA of $9.0 million, EBIT of $6.5 million and net income of $4.2 million, and it has $12 million of debt and $2 million of cash. A buyer uses Morrow & Pike and Harbour Street as peers. What is the equity worth?

scenes.head: Pricing a private café chain from listed peers

segs.say: Step 1. Peer EV/EBITDA: 10.66 and 8.02, average 9.34. Enterprise value 9.34 × 9.0 = $84.1 million; equity 84.1 − 12 + 2 = $74.1 million.
Step 2. Peer EV/EBIT: 13.67 and 11.34, average 12.51. Enterprise value $81.3 million; equity $71.3 million.
Step 3. Peer P/E: 17.99 and 12.74, average 15.37. Equity directly: 15.37 × 4.2 = $64.5 million (no bridge: P/E already prices the equity).
Step 4. The range across the two peers’ EV/EBITDA alone is $62.2 million (Harbour Street’s 8.0) to $85.9 million (Morrow & Pike’s 10.7).
Step 5. Two slips to avoid: applying the average P/E to EBITDA gives $138.3 million, and stopping at the $84.1 million enterprise value overstates the equity by the $10 million of net debt.

scenes.head: Pricing a private café chain from listed peers

segs.say: Roughly $64 million to $74 million for the equity from the averages, within a wider range of about $62 million to $86 million depending on which peer is closer.

Neither peer runs cafés, Copperkettle is far smaller, and its shares cannot be sold on an exchange. The buyer would weigh these before choosing a point in the range, and would check it with a DCF of Copperkettle’s own cash flows.

scenes.head: Copperkettle Coffee by an EV/EBITDA multiple

segs.say: Price Copperkettle Coffee by an EV/EBITDA multiple. Move the multiple between the two peers’ (8.0 and 10.7) and watch how much the equity moves. Then look at the P/E the result implies: if it is far outside the peers’ 12.7 to 18.0, the EV multiple and the earnings are telling different stories. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: What a P/E and a price-to-book should be

segs.say: The Gordon-implied P/E and price-to-book. Start at Morrow & Pike’s figures, then set Harbour Street’s (payout 42.5%, ROE 10.3%, cost of equity 11.08%). Raise the ROE above the cost of equity and see the price-to-book cross 1. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: Mixing equity and enterprise multiples

segs.say: Mixing equity and enterprise multiples. A P/E applied to EBITDA, or EV/EBITDA applied to net income, prices the wrong claimants’ cash. Match the numerator and denominator: equity value with earnings after interest, enterprise value with operating figures before interest.

scenes.head: Forgetting the bridge

segs.say: Forgetting the bridge. An EV multiple times EBITDA is an enterprise value. Subtract debt and add cash before dividing by the shares or comparing with a market capitalisation.

scenes.head: Calling a low multiple cheap

segs.say: Calling a low multiple cheap. Harbour Street’s 12.7 times earnings is below Morrow & Pike’s 18.0, but on its risk and return on equity the Gordon model justifies only about 8.7. Ask why a multiple is low before calling it a bargain.

scenes.head: Peers chosen for convenience

segs.say: Peers chosen for convenience. A peer group drawn from the same broad sector but different business models (a roaster and a food maker to price a café chain) can be the best available but still needs adjusting. Say why each peer is comparable and how it differs.

scenes.head: Averaging with outliers or mismatched years

segs.say: Averaging with outliers or mismatched years. One peer on a P/E of 60 after a bad year drags a mean far from the typical company. Use the median, the same year for every company, and earnings without one-off items.

scenes.head: Investment bankers’ comparables.

segs.say: Investment bankers’ comparables. When a company floats on a stock exchange, its advisers propose a price range largely from the multiples of listed peers, adjusted for differences in growth and size. The DCF in the prospectus work is a cross-check, and investors who buy in the offering test the range against the same peers.

scenes.head: Buying a small business.

segs.say: Buying a small business. Brokers who sell cafés, bakeries and practices usually quote a multiple of profit: of EBITDA for larger ones, of the owner’s earnings for small ones. Ana’s accountant uses one when he values a business for a client, then asks what the multiple assumes about growth and how much the owner’s own work is part of the profit, since a buyer will have to pay someone to do it.

scenes.head: A fund analyst’s screen.

segs.say: A fund analyst’s screen. An analyst at an equity fund sorts her sector by EV/EBITDA and P/E each month, not to buy the cheapest but to choose which companies deserve a closer look: a low multiple with a good return on capital is interesting; a low multiple with a poor return is usually a fair price. The screen starts the work; the fundamental analysis does it.

scenes.head: What to remember

segs.say: A multiple prices one company by what the market pays for similar ones; it is relative, so a mispriced sector misprices every member.

Equity multiples (P/E, price-to-book, dividend yield) use equity values and shareholders’ figures; enterprise multiples (EV/EBITDA, EV/EBIT) use enterprise value and operating figures. Never mix them.
An EV multiple gives enterprise value: subtract debt and add cash to reach the equity.
Morrow & Pike: P/E 18.0, EV/EBITDA 10.7, price-to-book 2.15. Harbour Street: 12.7, 8.0 and 1.31.
Justified P/E = payout × (1 + g) ÷ (r_E − g); justified price-to-book = ROE × justified P/E. Higher growth, lower risk and higher ROE justify higher multiples.
Harbour Street’s lower multiple is more than explained by its risk and its ROE below the cost of equity: low is not cheap.
Choose peers on business, growth, risk and size; use medians and ranges; adjust for one-offs, cycles and accounting.

scenes.head: Work the guided problems, then take the knowledge check.

segs.say: That is the whole lesson. Now work the guided problems, with hints when you need them, then try the questions on your own and take the knowledge check. A score of 80 percent completes the lesson.
